name: Non-Repudiation
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Signature You Cannot Later Take Back
lesson.summary: Non-repudiation is the property that a signer cannot credibly deny having authored a signed message, because only their private key could have produced a signature that verifies against their public key over the unaltered content.
lesson.body:
Data integrity, from the previous chapter, tells you whether a piece of data has changed. It says nothing about who is responsible for the data in the first place, and that gap matters enormously the moment money, contracts, or accountability are involved. Non-repudiation closes that gap: it is the property that once someone has signed a message with their private key, they cannot later credibly claim they did not send it or did not agree to it. This combines the previous two chapters directly, using a digital signature to bind a specific, integrity-protected message to a specific identity in a way that is hard to walk back.

The reason this works comes down to a contrast with an older, weaker approach: shared-secret authentication codes, sometimes called message authentication codes or MACs. A MAC lets two parties who both know the same secret key verify that a message came from someone holding that key, and that it has not been altered. But because both parties know the same secret, either one could have produced a valid MAC on any message, which means a MAC alone cannot prove which of the two actually sent it. A digital signature avoids this by relying on an asymmetric key pair rather than a shared secret. Only the private key holder can produce a valid signature, while anyone can verify it using the public key, so the set of people who could plausibly have created the signature shrinks to exactly one, assuming the private key was never exposed.

Because the signature is computed over a hash of the message, the same collision and preimage resistance properties covered earlier apply here too: a signer cannot later claim the content was different from what they actually signed, since any different content would produce a different hash and invalidate the signature. This is what makes the combination of data integrity and non-repudiation so powerful together. A valid signature over a message proves not just that the signer approved something, but that they approved this exact content, unaltered.

Bitcoin transactions are a clean real-world instance of this. When Alice signs a transaction spending her coins, that signature, produced with her private key, becomes attached to the transaction permanently once it is confirmed on the chain. She cannot later tell a court or a counterparty that she never authorized the transfer, because the cryptographic proof that only her key could have produced is sitting right there in the transaction record. It is worth being honest about the limits of this guarantee, though. Non-repudiation is only as strong as private key custody. If a private key is stolen, someone else can produce a signature indistinguishable from the legitimate owner's, and disputes over whether a key was actually stolen, or whether the true owner is simply denying a real transaction after the fact, are exactly the kind of messy real-world problem that pure cryptography cannot settle on its own.
